topic: Is it true we only use 10% of our brains? Fact-check it

slots.headline: You Already Use All of It
slots.body: Neuroscience confirms: we use virtually all of our brain, all the time. The myth that we only use 10% is a relic of early 20th-century misinterpretations — not hidden potential.

slots.headline: How the Myth Got Started
slots.body: In the early 1900s, psychologist William James speculated that we only use a fraction of our mental capacity. Later, self-help authors twisted that into the 10% claim. No actual brain study ever supported it.

slots.headline: Imaging Proves Full Use
slots.body:
• PET scans show activity throughout the brain, even during sleep
• fMRI scans detect blood flow changes across multiple regions during everyday tasks
• No area of the brain is truly inactive — resting states still show coordinated activity
• Brain disorders, not healthy inactivity, are what cause measurable dysfunction.
listItems: PET scans: Glucose uptake is high across the whole brain, even during rest.
fMRI: Most regions show activity within minutes, not just 10%.
Lesion studies: Even small damage can cause significant deficits — no silent 90%.

slots.headline: Self-Attention in 3 Steps
slots.body:
1. Create queries, keys, and values from each token embedding using learned weight matrices.
2. Score every token pair by taking the dot product of query and key, then scale by the square root of the key dimension.
3. Convert scores to weights with softmax and take the weighted sum of the values to produce each token’s contextual representation.

slides.body: Instead of one attention matrix, transformers run several attention heads in parallel. Each head can learn a different kind of relationship, and the layer combines those views into a richer representation.

slides.headline: Attention is computed as a weighted sum
slides.body: Self-attention scores how relevant each token is to every other token, then uses those scores as weights to blend token representations. Higher-weight tokens dominate the updated representation, so the model can directly pull information.

pairwise.reason: Carousel A provides a precise, step-by-step breakdown of transformer internals (tokens, embeddings, attention, layers, training) in a logical order that exactly matches the request for developers new to ML, while Carousel B drifts into history and scaling costs, missing key required elements like next-token prediction and ending on a tangent about mixture-of-experts rather than a solid understanding.
